subject: Biology
description: Covers Lysosomes, Plastids, and Mitochondrial DNA.

questions.stem: Which organelle is famously known as the 'Suicide Bag' of the cell?

options.option_text: Lysosome
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Golgi Apparatus

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing powerful digestive enzymes. They act as the cell's waste disposal system, digesting obsolete components, food particles, and engulfed viruses or bacteria. They are called "suicide bags" (or suicidal bags) because if a cell is damaged beyond repair, the lysosomes rupture and release their enzymes into the cell, entirely digesting (destroying) the cell itself in a process called autolysis.
DECOY BUSTING: Mitochondria are the 'Powerhouses' (making ATP). Ribosomes are the 'Protein Factories'. The Golgi apparatus is the 'Packaging Center'.
EXAM INSIGHT: The highly destructive enzymes inside a lysosome are called 'hydrolytic enzymes', and they only work effectively in an acidic environment (pH ~5.0).

questions.stem: Which of the following cellular components is found EXCLUSIVELY in plant cells and NOT in animal cells?

options.option_text: Plastids (like Chloroplasts)
Mitochondria
Nucleus
Cell Membrane

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Plastids are double-membrane organelles found only in plant and algal cells. The most famous plastid is the Chloroplast, which contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis. Other plastids include chromoplasts (which give fruits and flowers their colors) and leucoplasts (which store starch/oil). Animal cells do not photosynthesize, so they do not have plastids.
DECOY BUSTING: Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic, meaning they both have a Nucleus, Mitochondria, and a Cell Membrane (plasma membrane). However, plant cells ALSO have a rigid Cell Wall OUTSIDE the cell membrane, which animal cells lack.
EXAM INSIGHT: Another major difference is the vacuole. Plant cells typically have one massive central vacuole that takes up 50-90% of the cell volume, while animal cells have many small, temporary vacuoles.

questions.stem: The genetic material (DNA) of a eukaryotic cell is housed within the nucleus. However, DNA is also independently found in which other organelle?

options.option_text: Mitochondria
Ribosomes
Endoplasmic Reticulum
Lysosomes

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: While the vast majority of DNA is in the nucleus, the Mitochondria contain their own small, circular DNA (mtDNA). Because they have their own DNA and ribosomes, mitochondria are semi-autonomous and can replicate themselves independently of the cell. (In plants, Chloroplasts also have their own DNA).
DECOY BUSTING: Ribosomes are made of RNA and protein, not DNA. The ER and Lysosomes do not contain genetic material.
EXAM INSIGHT: According to the 'Endosymbiotic Theory', mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that were engulfed by a larger cell billions of years ago. A highly tested fact: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited strictly from the MOTHER.

questions.stem: The 'Fluid Mosaic Model' of the plasma membrane, which describes proteins floating in a phospholipid bilayer, was proposed by which pair of scientists?

options.option_text: Watson and Crick (1953, proposed the DNA double helix)
Singer and Nicolson (1972, fluid mosaic membrane model)
Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39, cell theory founders)
Robertson and Danielli (1935, protein-lipid sandwich model)

questions.explanation: Singer and Nicolson proposed the Fluid Mosaic Model in 1972, describing the membrane as a mosaic of proteins embedded in or attached to a fluid phospholipid bilayer. Robertson and Danielli proposed the earlier 'sandwich' or 'unit membrane' model which this replaced — a common distractor. Watson and Crick are associated with DNA, not membrane structure.

questions.stem: Which type of RNA molecule directly carries amino acids to the ribosome during the translation phase of protein synthesis?

options.option_text: mRNA (messenger RNA, carries genetic code from the nucleus)
tRNA (transfer RNA, ferries specific amino acids to the ribosome)
rRNA (ribosomal RNA, forms the catalytic core of the ribosome)
snRNA (small nuclear RNA, involved in pre-mRNA intron splicing)

questions.explanation: tRNA has an anticodon loop that pairs with mRNA codons and an acceptor stem that binds the corresponding amino acid, physically delivering it to the ribosomal A-site. mRNA is the template being read, not the amino-acid carrier. rRNA (along with protein) forms the ribosome itself and catalyses peptide bond formation but does not ferry amino acids.

questions.stem: The cell wall of true fungi (Kingdom Fungi) is primarily composed of which structural polymer, distinguishing them from both plants and bacteria?

options.option_text: Cellulose, the same β-1,4-glucose polymer as in plant cell walls
Chitin, a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine
Peptidoglycan, a polymer of amino-sugars found in bacterial walls
Lignin, the aromatic polymer that hardens secondary plant cell walls

questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls are built from chitin, the same polymer found in insect exoskeletons, but composed of N-acetylglucosamine units. This is a key taxonomic distinction: plants use cellulose, bacteria use peptidoglycan (murein), and lignin fortifies vascular plant xylem — none of these are the primary fungal wall component. Examiners frequently test this three-kingdom wall comparison.

questions.stem: Mitochondrial ribosomes in eukaryotic cells are structurally similar to prokaryotic ribosomes rather than to cytoplasmic ribosomes of the same cell. What sedimentation coefficient do mitochondrial ribosomes carry?

options.option_text: 80S — identical to cytoplasmic ribosomes of eukaryotic cells
70S — same as the ribosomes in prokaryotic bacterial cells
60S — the large subunit coefficient found near the nuclear pore
90S — the precursor ribosome assembled inside the nucleolus

questions.explanation: Mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S (made of 50S + 30S subunits), exactly like prokaryotic ribosomes, which is key evidence for the Endosymbiotic Theory — mitochondria evolved from engulfed aerobic bacteria. Cytoplasmic ribosomes of eukaryotes are 80S (60S + 40S). The 90S is a transient pre-ribosomal particle in the nucleolus; it is not a functional ribosome.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is performed EXCLUSIVELY by the Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) and not by the Rough ER?

options.option_text: Synthesising secretory proteins destined for export from the cell
Biosynthesis of lipids and steroid hormones in liver and gland cells
Providing ribosome attachment sites during active protein translation
Transporting newly synthesised proteins toward the Golgi apparatus

questions.explanation: SER lacks ribosomes and specialises in lipid synthesis, steroid hormone production (in adrenal cortex, gonads), and drug detoxification in liver cells. Rough ER is studded with ribosomes and synthesises secretory and membrane-bound proteins. Both RER and SER participate in transport toward the Golgi; but lipid/steroid biosynthesis is the SER's exclusive hallmark.

questions.stem: During Prophase I of meiosis, crossing over (exchange of DNA segments between non-sister chromatids) physically occurs at which sub-stage?

options.option_text: Leptotene — chromosomes first condense as thin, thread-like structures
Pachytene — bivalents are fully synapsed and crossing over takes place
Zygotene — homologous chromosomes begin lateral synapsis side-by-side
Diplotene — synaptonemal complex dissolves and chiasmata become visible

questions.explanation: Crossing over (recombination) occurs during Pachytene, when homologs are fully paired via the synaptonemal complex forming bivalents (tetrads). The most tempting distractor is Diplotene — chiasmata become VISIBLE then because the synaptonemal complex dissolves, but the DNA exchange already happened at Pachytene. Leptotene = condensation; Zygotene = synapsis beginning.

questions.stem: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump is essential for maintaining the resting membrane potential of neurons and muscle cells. For every single ATP molecule it hydrolyses, what is the precise ion exchange it carries out?

options.option_text: Pumps 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed
Pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed
Pumps 3 Na⁺ into and 2 K⁺ out of the cell per ATP hydrolysed
Pumps equal 2 Na⁺ and 2 K⁺ in opposite directions per ATP hydrolysed

questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is an electrogenic antiporter: per ATP it ejects 3 Na⁺ outward and imports 2 K⁺ inward, creating a net negative charge inside (contributing to the −70 mV resting potential). The '2 Na⁺ out / 3 K⁺ in' option is the classic reversal-confusion trap. The directions are fixed — Na⁺ always exits, K⁺ always enters — ruling out option C. The 2:2 option incorrectly implies electrogenically neutral exchange.
